say.en: A notice on the college gate is for everyone; a note inside your classroom is only for your class. Variables also have such boundaries, called scope. In this lesson: Tell local from global variables.
Use the global keyword correctly.

body.en: A variable defined outside every function is a *global* variable; it can be read anywhere in the program. A variable defined inside a function is a local variable; it exists only while the function runs and only inside it.
body.kn: ಎಲ್ಲಾ ಫಂಕ್ಷನ್‌ಗಳ ಹೊರಗೆ ವ್ಯಾಖ್ಯಾನಿಸಿದ ವೇರಿಯಬಲ್ ಗ್ಲೋಬಲ್; ಅದನ್ನು ಎಲ್ಲಿ ಬೇಕಾದರೂ ಓದಬಹುದು. ಫಂಕ್ಷನ್ ಒಳಗೆ ವ್ಯಾಖ್ಯಾನಿಸಿದ ವೇರಿಯಬಲ್ ಲೋಕಲ್; ಅದು ಆ ಫಂಕ್ಷನ್ ಒಳಗೆ ಮಾತ್ರ ಇರುತ್ತದೆ.

heading.en: Scope of Variables and Passing Mutable Objects

tagline.en: Local and global scope, the global keyword, UnboundLocalError, and why a function can change a list you pass but not an int.

myth.en: Inside a function I can write z = z + 1 to update a global z, because the function can see globals.

truth.en: Because z is assigned in the function, it is local there, and reading it before it has a value raises UnboundLocalError. Add global z at the top of the function, or pass z in and return the new value. Reading a global without assigning does work, so learners think updating works too. The assignment is what changes the name's scope for the whole function.

say.en: Global: made at top level, readable anywhere. Local: made inside a function, lives only during the call.
Assigning to a name in a function makes it local, unless declared global.
Using a local name before giving it a value raises UnboundLocalError.
Changes to a list or dict in place are seen by the caller; rebinding a parameter is not.
Default values are made once, so avoid mutable defaults.

goal.en: Local and global scope, the global keyword, UnboundLocalError, and why a function can change a list you pass but not an int.

question.en: What is printed? def total(): x = 3; x += 1; return x then x = 7 and print(total() + x)

explain.en: The local x inside total() becomes 4 and is returned; the global x is still 7; 4 + 7 = 11.

task.en: What is nums after def f(L): L = [0] and f(nums) with nums = [5, 6]?

question.en: What is nums after def f(L): L = [0] and f(nums) with nums = [5, 6]?

explain.en: L = [0] only makes the local name L point at a new list. The original list is not changed in place, so nums is still [5, 6].

takeaway.en: Global: made at top level, readable anywhere. Local: made inside a function, lives only during the call.

narration.en: Many people think: Inside a function I can write z = z + 1 to update a global z, because the function can see globals. Actually: Because z is assigned in the function, it is local there, and reading it before it has a value raises UnboundLocalError. Add global z at the top of the function, or pass z in and return the new value. Reading a global without assigning does work, so learners think updating works too. The assignment is what changes the name's scope for the whole function.

num changed to 10

num equals 5.
def myfunc().
global num.
print("Accessing num =", num).
num equals 10.
print("num changed to", num).
myfunc().
print("Outside, num =", num).
Because of global num, the assignment num equals 10 changes the global variable.

So the answer is Accessing num equals 5
num changed to 10
Outside, num equals 10.

body.en: When Python meets a name inside a function, it looks for a local name first, then (for nested functions) the enclosing one, then the global one, and finally built-in names: L-E-G-B.
